title: Concurrency limits and streaming edge-case demo
summary: Short technical walkthrough focusing on long context handling, high TPS concurrency, streaming backpressure and failure modes. SE demoed console + API, showed optimize suggestions, and discussed fallback strategies. Agreed next steps: run a staged load test, share private deployment checklist, and deliver SLO/benchmark spreadsheet.
topics: Long context window behavior (prefix caching, kv cache eviction)
High TPS and concurrency profiles (autoscale, reserved pools)
Timeout and retry strategies; graceful degradation
Console demo: tracing, per-token latency, Optimize suggestions
Security and deployment notes (VPC, KMS, SOC2)
transcript:
[00:00] Ari (AE): Hi everyone, thanks for taking the time. We, uh, wanted to run through a focused edge-case demo — long context and high concurrency plus streaming backpressure.
[00:14] Raj (Customer): Yep, thanks. We bumped into an issue on Friday where stream responses started dropping after about 3k concurrent sessions. Not sure if it was a client issue or you know, the endpoint.
[00:30] Maya (SE): Cool — we'll reproduce similar conditions. Quick agenda: 1) console walk-through for trace + token profiling, 2) API demo showing streaming under load, 3) discuss timeouts and fallback policies, 4) next steps. Sound ok?
[00:45] Sara (Customer): Sounds good. We're mostly on k8s in GCP, and using a mix of hosted endpoints and a dedicated pool for user-facing tasks.
[00:58] Raj: Also, we do long-document tasks — some sessions push 200k token contexts because of multi-document chat transcripts. That seems to trigger kv cache thrash.
[01:14] Maya: Right. For long contexts we demo prefix caching and kv cache shrink behavior. Important to note — we sometimes quote the kv cache as "kay-vee" in docs but the runtime logs show it as kvcache, so transcription note: logs may read differently.
[01:30] Ari: Ok let's jump into the console. I'll share the deck and the console — I put the demo workspace link in the chat: https://redwood.example/demo/blueharbor-edge.
[01:45] [screen share starts] Maya: Here is the model route configured with a dedicated pool. You can see the token latency breakdown, per-route token counts and batching efficiency. The green blocks are served from prefix cache.
[02:09] Raj: That cache hit rate looks good but when we hit the big sessions it drops to 12%. Is that expected?
[02:20] Maya: It depends on the context overlap. If you have shared prefixes across sessions the cache helps a lot. For highly unique tokens across 200k token sessions we see low reuse and higher memory churn; that triggers KV eviction earlier.
[02:37] Lina: What's the practical limit for single-session context? We saw a hard stop near 512k tokens in our test environment.
[02:45] Maya: Architecturally we support up to the model's context limit; performance degrades sublinearly. In practice beyond ~300–400k tokens you'll see tail latency spikes and memory pressure unless you use chunking or summarization. We usually recommend streaming summaries into a shorter context and keeping a moving window.
[03:04] Raj: Ok, show us how streaming behaves under concurrent load.
[03:11] Maya: Switching to the API load test harness. I'm going to start a synthetic client pushing a thousand concurrent streaming sessions at 120 TPS average per instance to simulate your Friday pattern.
[03:26] [sound of keyboard]
[03:33] Maya: Starting now — note the trace panel on the right. You can see the gRPC streams open and the server-side backpressure metrics.
[03:45] [00:04:00 marker in UI] Maya: We already see some stream stalls; the client-side shows stalled writes and the server indicates output_queue_full events, which is backpressure at the runtime output buffer.
[04:01] Raj: Hmm, the client library retries every 2s by default — that caused some duplicate tokens in our logs last time.
[04:10] Ari: That's a common pattern. We recommend a single-shot idempotency token per request for non-chat operations and a circuit-breaker-based retry for streaming.
[04:24] Lina: Can you show fallback policies? We want to degrade gracefully to a smaller model or to cached replies rather than fail.
[04:33] Maya: Sure. In the route config you can specify fallback_chain: first attempt full model, then tpe-quantized small model, then cached_response. I'll toggle to a canary that uses that policy.
[04:47] [toggle change] Maya: Now, on peak we see automatic routing to the smaller variant — note the latency jump is milder and cost drops.
[04:59] Raj: Is this automatic or do we need Dedicated?
[05:05] Maya: It can work in Hosted but we recommend Dedicated for predictable throughput; Dedicated lets you reserve capacity at the GPU pool level so autoscale actions have headroom. For graceful fallback you can still rely on hosted model variants and routing.
[05:20] Sara: Are there logs for when fallback triggers? We need auditability for SRE.
[05:27] Maya: Yes — every routing decision is logged with reason_code and token counts; available in the console and via the logs API.
[05:36] Raj: Backpressure — when the output_queue_full happened earlier, did the server drop frames or delay them?
[05:44] Maya: It delays sends and will throttle upstream requests by applying a soft accept limit. If a client holds the HTTP stream open and the server can't keep up, the client sees increased tail latency and may trigger client-side timeouts. If you set explicit socket timeouts too tight you get partial responses.
[06:00] Raj: So best practice is to keep client timeouts long and implement a streaming health ping?
[06:07] Maya: Exactly. Keep the client timeout higher than expected p99 latency and use a heartbeat message. Also tune your retry backoff and idempotency.
[06:17] Lina: Do you recommend chunk size? Our team splits docs into 8k token chunks right now.
[06:23] Maya: That's reasonable. For very long docs we recommend 4–8k chunks with summarization, and maintain a short context window of ~32–64k for the active conversational state.
[06:36] [08:00 on UI timeline] Maya: I'm going to push the TPS up now to see how the runtime responds under a sudden surge.
[06:45] [keyboard]
[06:52] Maya: Ramp is live: 120 -> 600 -> 2,000 TPS across 2,000 concurrent sessions.
[07:02] Raj: We're seeing timeouts at the client after ~18s, which matches our production alerts.
[07:08] Maya: On our trace the p95 jumps to 3.2s then p99 to 17.1s, so those client timeouts align with the p99 tail. You'll also see more out-of-order partial streams when preemption occurs during heavy GC.
[07:27] Raj: GC? Are you on JVM somewhere?
[07:30] Maya: Sorry — I mean runtime memory cleanup on the serving process, not JVM-specific. The model runtime does internal memory reclamation and compacting which can cause short stalls. We log those as memory_compaction events.
[07:46] Lina: Does quantization impact streaming? We tried 4-bit quant but saw jitter.
[07:52] Maya: Lower-bit quant can increase throughput but sometimes increases variance in generation time per token depending on kernel selection. For steady streaming with low jitter we recommend 8-bit hybrid profiles unless cost forces the 4-bit path, then pair with stronger batching to reduce variance.
[08:11] Sara: Can we simulate our client library artifact — it uses HTTP chunked with a small write buffer and aggressive reconnects.
[08:20] Maya: We'll drop a sample client config in the repo and run a realistic replay. I want to show one more thing: in Optimize we have a recommendation panel — it's suggesting increasing batch cap for this route and enabling kv prefix compression for similar docs. If we apply that, watch the cache hit rate climb.
[08:40] [applies suggestion]
[08:47] Maya: Cache hit rate jumps to ~38% in the synthetic replay, which lowers per-token compute and stabilizes tail latency.
[08:55] Raj: Nice. What about timeouts in dedicated pools if you run out of GPUs?
[09:02] Maya: If Dedicated pool capacity is exhausted and no burst is allowed, the router will either queue requests briefly or fail-fast based on your route policy; you can set route.sla.timeout_behavior to queue|fail|fallback.
[09:18] Lina: We prefer queueing for short spikes but fail-fast to fallback for longer.
[09:23] Ari: That matches what we see in enterprise patterns.
[09:28] Raj: Ok, show us a failure mode where the stream is partially emitted — we had COMMIT-like partials in our logs and debugging was a pain.
[09:35] Maya: Triggering a mid-stream cancellation now.
[09:39] [simulated cancel] Maya: The server emitted a partial chunk and logged stream_cancelled_by_client with offset 12,345 tokens. For these we store a truncated KV checkpoint and expose an srid for later resume only if you set route.resume.enabled=true. Otherwise the session is closed.
[09:59] Raj: We did not have resume enabled — that explains our truncated sessions.
[10:04] Lina: Do you keep partial traces for audit?
[10:07] Maya: We keep the traces and partial token counts; full token payloads are only retained per your retention policy and compliance settings. For enterprise you can set log.retention.policy to keep tokens for X days or route to your S3.
[10:22] Sara: Let's walk through recommended retry/backoff policy.
[10:27] Maya: We recommend exponential backoff with jitter: initial_backoff 500ms, max 10s, and cap retries to 3. For streaming, prefer connection-level retries rather than re-sending the entire prompt to avoid double-charging. Use idempotency tokens for non-streaming calls.
[10:46] Raj: Any tooling to detect duplicate tokens? We had doubled responses a few times.
[10:50] Ari: The logging includes request_id and token_start offsets; our analytics can detect overlapping token ranges and flag probable duplicates. We'll share a notebook to run anomaly detection on your logs.
[11:05] Lina: Security quick check — SOC2, SSO, KMS?
[11:10] Ari: We are SOC 2 Type II; we support SAML/SSO, RBAC via the console, and KMS integrations for private deployments. For on-prem or VPC you can bring your own HSM. We'll attach the security pack in the follow-up.
[11:25] Raj: Great. So what's next?
[11:29] Maya: Proposed next steps in the chat: 1) run a staged load test from your staging IPs (we'll provide the harness), 2) share the private deployment checklist and security pack, 3) deliver the benchmark spreadsheet with SLO columns filled, 4) set up a canary trial on a dedicated small pool.
[11:48] Ari: I'll capture those now. Anything else?
[11:52] Sara: Could you also include recommended client library config for chunking & timeouts?
[11:57] Maya: Yes — we'll add a sample HTTP chunked config and a sample gRPC streaming config.
[12:05] Raj: One more ask — can you run the load test with our real payloads (masked) to reproduce the kv thrash?
[12:12] Maya: Absolutely — we just need a sanitized subset. We'll run with your masked dataset in our isolated staging so we don't log sensitive tokens.
[12:21] [summary recap] Ari: Recap: we'll run the load test, share security docs and recommended client configs, provide benchmark sheet and run a small dedicated canary. Maya will own the load test executions. We'll aim to post results and action items by next Thursday.
[12:38] Raj: Great, thanks both.
[12:41] [end screen share]
[12:45] Maya: Wrapping up — adding links: demo workspace (https://redwood.example/demo/blueharbor-edge), load harness repo (https://git.redwood.example/blueharbor-replay), security pack (s3://redwood-sec/blueharbor-secsumm.pdf).
[12:58] Ari: Thanks, everyone.
[13:02] Sara: Thanks, bye.
next_steps: Maya to run staged load test using customer's masked payloads and shared harness; target completion: 2026-09-16
Ari to send security pack and private deployment checklist via email (include SAML/KMS docs)
Maya to share benchmark spreadsheet with p50/p95/p99 SLO columns populated
Schedule canary trial for dedicated small GPU pool for week of 2026-09-21
